details:
**Charge of the Light Brigade**
A disastrous British cavalry attack at the Battle of Balaclava on October 25, 1854. A vague order from the commander Lord Raglan, passed on by Captain Nolan and the Earl of Lucan, sent the Earl of Cardigan's Light Brigade of about 600 men straight down the North Valley into massed Russian artillery, and the brigade suffered heavy losses. Alfred, Lord Tennyson's poem "The Charge of the Light Brigade" ("Half a league, half a league, / Half a league onward... Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred") made it famous.

**Florence Nightingale, the "Lady with the Lamp"**
A British nurse who led a team of nurses to the army hospital at the Selimiye Barracks in Scutari, across the Bosporus from Constantinople. She greatly improved sanitation and earned her nickname by making night rounds of the wards. She used her "rose" or "coxcomb" diagrams, a kind of polar area chart, to show that disease killed far more soldiers than battle wounds.

**Siege of Sevastopol**
The central campaign of the war, an allied siege of Russia's main Black Sea naval base from October 1854 to September 1855, lasting about eleven months. It ended when French troops stormed the key Malakoff Redoubt, after which the Russians blew up their fortifications and scuttled their fleet before abandoning the city.

**"Thin Red Line"**
At Balaclava, Sir Colin Campbell's 93rd (Sutherland) Highlanders, in their red coats, formed a line only two men deep and drove off a Russian cavalry attack on the British base. The journalist William Howard Russell described them as a "thin red streak," and the phrase became "the thin red line."

**Battle of Balaclava**
The October 1854 battle in which Russian forces tried to cut the British off from their supply port at Balaclava during the siege of Sevastopol. It featured three famous actions: the Thin Red Line, the successful Charge of the Heavy Brigade, and the disastrous Charge of the Light Brigade.

**Battles of the Alma and Inkerman**
The Alma (September 1854) was the first major battle on the Crimean Peninsula. British and French troops under Lord Raglan and Marshal Armand de Saint-Arnaud forced Prince Menshikov's Russians from the heights above the river, including the area near Telegraph Hill. Inkerman (November 1854) was a confused battle in thick fog, sometimes called "the soldiers' battle," with fierce fighting around the "Sandbag Battery." Menshikov's attempt to break the siege of Sevastopol failed.

**Mary Seacole and the "British Hotel"**
A Jamaican-born nurse and businesswoman who, after being turned down for Nightingale's nursing corps, paid her own way to the Crimea. Near Balaclava she set up the "British Hotel," where she sold food and supplies to officers and treated sick and wounded soldiers with herbal remedies.

**Roger Fenton's "The Valley of the Shadow of Death"**
Fenton, one of the first war photographers, documented the conflict with the backing of the publisher Thomas Agnew & Sons. His best-known image shows a desolate road covered with cannonballs, and its title quotes Psalm 23. A second version with no cannonballs on the road has raised long debate over whether the scene was staged. Combined with William Howard Russell's reports for The Times, this made the Crimean War one of the first wars covered by modern media.

**Lord Raglan**
The British commander-in-chief, a veteran of Wellington's staff who had lost an arm at Waterloo. His ambiguous order at Balaclava led to the Charge of the Light Brigade, and he was widely blamed for the army's supply failures in the first winter. He died of illness during the siege in 1855.

**Battle of Sinop (Sinope)**
In November 1853, a Russian fleet under Admiral Pavel Nakhimov destroyed an Ottoman squadron in the harbor of Sinop on the Black Sea, using explosive shells. Only the steamer Taif escaped. It was the last major naval battle involving sailing ships, and the British and French public's outrage at the "massacre" helped bring both countries into the war in 1854.

**Causes: Holy Land sites, the Danubian Principalities, and the Straits**
The war grew out of a dispute between France, which protected Catholics, and Russia, which protected Orthodox Christians, over control of holy sites in Palestine. France sent the warship Charlemagne to the Dardanelles in apparent violation of the 1841 London Straits Convention, and Tsar Nicholas I then demanded to be recognized as protector of the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects and occupied Moldavia and Wallachia. During the Danube campaign that followed, the Russians besieged Silistra.

**Treaty of Paris (1856)**
The peace that ended the war in Russia's defeat. It neutralized the Black Sea, banning warships and naval arsenals there, guaranteed the Ottoman Empire's territory, and placed the Danubian Principalities under the joint protection of the great powers. A separate convention demilitarized the Åland Islands.

**Siege of Kars**
The last major action of the war, in the Caucasus in 1855. The British officer William Fenwick Williams led the Ottoman garrison of Kars through a months-long Russian siege. Omar Pasha's relief expedition arrived too late, and the starving town surrendered in November 1855.

**Baltic and Pacific campaigns**
The war spread beyond the Black Sea. In the Baltic, a British fleet under Charles Napier joined the French in capturing and destroying the Russian fortress of Bomarsund in the Åland Islands, and British ships shelled Russian positions on the island of Gogland. In the far north, an allied squadron bombarded the White Sea coast, and in the Pacific an allied attack on Petropavlovsk on Kamchatka was driven back.

**Battle of Kinburn and other "firsts"**
At Kinburn in 1855, French armored floating batteries bombarded Russian forts, one of the first combat uses of ironclad warships. The war also saw early use of the telegraph and railways in war, Nikolay Pirogov's advances in field surgery and anesthesia, Alexis Soyer's field stove, Isambard Kingdom Brunel's prefabricated hospital at Renkioi, and the creation of the Victoria Cross. Piedmont-Sardinia also sent about 15,000 troops under Alfonso La Marmora to join the allies.
